commit 2321a6aae9f1ca9fa20b3fdb7cc00cea200544f8
Author: Diogenesoftoronto <diogenesoft@protonmail.com>
Date:   Mon Jun 15 23:11:20 2026 -0400

    Fix Railway build: explicit railpack layer inputs + Convex deploy in build
    
    Newer Railpack no longer auto-mounts local source into custom steps, so
    `bun install --frozen-lockfile` ran in an empty context and failed with
    "could not find a package.json". Declare explicit `local` layer inputs on the
    install step (package.json + bun.lock) and the build step (full tree minus
    node_modules).
    
    Run `npx convex deploy --cmd '<frontend build>'` in the build step so the
    backend deploys with each Railway push, gated on CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY (degrades
    to a frontend-only build when unset). Document CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY and setting
    server-side Convex secrets via `npx convex env set --prod`.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Railway build step: deploy Convex backend (when key is configured), then
# build the Qwik City frontend + SSR server.
#
# Gating: when CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY is unset (frontend-only deploys, preview
# environments, local re-runs) we still build the frontend but skip the
# backend push.

set -euo pipefail

if [ -n "${CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY:-}" ]; then
  echo "==> Deploying Convex backend"
  # 1.46 fixes index-removal review with deploy-only keys. Keep CI deployment
  # tooling explicit even when the app's lockfile pins an older client.
  npx --yes convex@1.46.0 deploy --cmd 'bun run build.client && bun run build.server'
else
  echo "==> CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY not set — building frontend only, skipping convex deploy"
  bun run build.client
  bun run build.server
fi
  -e, --environment <ENVIRONMENT>  Environment to link to
  -p, --project <PROJECT>          Project to link to
  -s, --service <SERVICE>          The service to link to

items.text: what ports does devenv up open
I’ll check the devenv configuration for services and their ports.

`devenv up` starts:

- **5180** — Qwik/Vite app at http://127.0.0.1:5180
- **6010** — Storybook at http://127.0.0.1:6010
- **Convex dev** — uses the configured cloud deployment; no local backend port.

Both UI servers bind to loopback. Override their ports with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT` and `TWYNE_STORYBOOK_PORT`.

Defined in [devenv.nix](/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/devenv.nix:162).
hey there are many components missing in the storybook that I  would like you to add please
I’ll compare the app’s components with the existing stories, then add coverage for the missing components using the current Storybook conventions.
I’m using the Impeccable skill to keep the new stories consistent with Twyne’s UI and design conventions.
specifically the modal cards in the  editor
Got it. I’ll focus on the editor’s modal cards and popovers, including their interactive and empty states.

The missing cards are the persona-note conversation, proposed-edit decision, and writer margin-note thread. I’ll add stories for each, with reply, resolve, accept, strike, and dismiss actions working in local preview state. I also found the code-line highlighting modal missing from the existing insertion stories.

The three card families now have 23 stories covering drafts, conversations, evidence, reply failures, streaming states, mobile layouts, and margin placement. The two code-line modal stories are also added. TypeScript and lint checks pass; I’m checking browser interactions and the production Storybook build next.

The shared preview can read and type into the stories, but its snapshot and click calls repeatedly time out: “Preview automation snapshot timed out after 15000ms” and “Preview automation click timed out after 5000ms.” I’m switching to a local browser check to verify the interactions.

Browser testing caught a missing auth/client context around the cards’ read-aloud buttons. I’ve added the same signed-out provider setup used by other stories. The insertion modals and persona-card states checked so far now render without those errors; the remaining card states and interaction checks are running.

The core interactions pass in the browser: placing and replying to writer notes, resolving and reopening them, replying to and striking persona notes, and accepting or striking proposed edits. The persona card also fits at phone width. I’m finishing the remaining state checks and static build.
include the selection ui for when a person writes and that part of the text is selected by the personanote
I’ll add a manuscript story where you can type and select text to open the selection toolbar, then click a persona-marked passage to see its note card beside it.
inclcude the ui for the quick mark ruule estimate of what i am getting and theh section stuff
I’ll trace those controls in the editor and add their stories too: the quick-mark estimate, ruler, and section controls.

I’m treating “quick mark” as the rubric’s estimated grade and criteria breakdown. I’ve added the ruler and a section-navigation story with a real editable document, so margin changes and section reordering can be tried directly.

The selection stories now support typing, text selection, both toolbar menus, and opening the persona note from its marked passage. The quick-mark stories show simulated grades, criterion details, and weighting controls; their grading buttons stay in preview mode and make no provider requests.

The quick-mark controls, ruler adjustment, section navigation, and section reordering all pass browser checks. The quick-mark check also recorded zero external requests and zero IndexedDB writes while changing criteria and pressing the grading actions. I’m checking the remaining layouts and the final build.

There are now 45 added stories across the modal cards, selection tools, quick-mark rubric, ruler, and sections. TypeScript, lint, formatting, and 80 focused rubric tests pass. The static build is still running; the previous build took about five minutes, mostly in Storybook’s Qwik documentation plugin.

The added UI variants have rendered without browser errors, including the mobile selection, note, section, and quick-mark layouts. I’m waiting for the static build, then checking that its packaged stories work too.

Added **45 Storybook stories**, including:

- Editor modal cards: persona notes, proposed edits, and writer comments.
- [Text selection and persona-marked passages](http://localhost:6010/?path=/story/editor-selectionactions--persona-marked-passage).
- [Quick-mark grade estimates and criteria](http://localhost:6010/?path=/story/rubric-quickmark--estimated-grade).
- Interactive ruler, section navigation, and reordering.

Build, TypeScript, lint, formatting, 80 tests, and browser checks passed. Grades use clearly labelled simulated fixtures.

For “quick mark,” do you mean the rubric’s estimated grade and criteria breakdown?
i thought both were the same but i think putting them both in the storybook is important
Yes, both belong in Storybook. The rubric estimate is already there; I’ll add the inline quick-review UI too, including its expandable finding and unavailable states.
I found two inline surfaces: the expandable status above the manuscript, and the `?` marker that opens passage feedback. I’ll include both, using the production renderer with simulated findings.

The inline stories now use the actual `?` marker and feedback popover, alongside the expandable status. The shared preview still reports “Preview automation snapshot timed out after 15000ms,” so I’m checking the interactions with the local browser fallback.

I’ve added 13 inline-review stories covering the four finding types, tentative feedback, the open popover, waiting and checking states, no issue found, and unavailable states. The focused tests pass, including a regression check that a reused marker still opens and cleans up its popover correctly.

The status expands, the `?` marker opens passage feedback, dismissal removes it, and editing clears the old decoration. I’m finishing the unavailable-state and mobile checks, then checking the packaged Storybook build.
the marked passage in the real editor has a clickable red button at the end of the text that is missing  here.
I’ll check the real editor’s marker code and add the same end-of-passage button to the manuscript story.

The story was missing the production `MarkAnchorWidgets` extension. I’ve added it and matched the real editor’s click behavior: clicking the marked text places the caret; clicking the red button opens the persona note.

The red button now opens the note in the story. Testing also found that Enter was being handled by the editor instead of activating the focused button. I’m fixing that in the shared widget so keyboard activation works in both the story and the app.

The red button passes mouse, Enter, and Space activation checks, and the note card fits on mobile. TypeScript, lint, formatting, and the five focused marker/review tests pass. I’m checking the remaining inline-review states and waiting for the static build.

The stories now distinguish the three surfaces: the red dot opens a persona note, the `?` opens quick passage feedback, and the rubric shows the whole-draft grade estimate. Both passage buttons use the real editor widgets.
The packaged Storybook passes the red-button click and keyboard checks too. The inline-review stories are also passing in the static build, including dismissal/reset and unavailable states.

Fixed the [missing red button](http://localhost:6010/?path=/story/editor-selectionactions--persona-note-anchor). It opens the persona note with click, Enter, or Space.

**Where Twyne already is.** Most of the plumbing exists:
- **Desktop app:** it already runs a local model server, `desktop/litert-server.ts`.
- **Local text models:** `evals/run-local-model.ts` already tests LFM2.5-2.6B as the local engine, served through llama.cpp's `llama-server --jinja`.
- **Voice parts:** speech output already runs in the browser (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`). The Live voice desk is separate from the provider: the tools, edit proposals and apply/discard steps live in `live-voice-contract` and `live-voice-workspace`. A local voice model could reuse all of that.

**What I could confirm about LFM3** (the release is a day old, so coverage is thin):
- **Sizes and cost:** the audio model and Omni are about 2B parameters. The hosted API charges $2 per million audio-input tokens and $10 per million audio-output tokens. Liquid says the first response token can arrive about 50ms after speech ends, but that's their best case.
- **Running it locally:** llama.cpp can run the text side, and speech-to-text is still a pending pull request there. Full two-way voice chat currently needs Liquid's Python runtime. I found nothing on running it in the browser (WebGPU/ONNX), and only one third-party blog mentions full-duplex at all.
- **Vision:** you're right that Twyne doesn't need it. Omni would mean downloading vision weights for nothing, so the audio-only model is the better pick.
- **The decision model:** I couldn't confirm "D1" from the sources I found. Can you send me a link?

**How I'd build it:**
1. **Desktop first.** Run LFM3 audio as a local server next to `litert-server` and point the Live relay at it with the same event shape. Live voice would then work offline and cost nothing on desktop.
2. **Web next.** The web version can't run the Python runtime, so voice there has to stay hosted until a WebGPU/ONNX build ships. One caveat on the out-of-credits fallback: it only works if the user has a local runtime (desktop, or a local server they set up).
3. **Use the decision model in place of Jev.** It would run the local `judgement` and `interpret` steps. That takes Jev's 503s and the per-action $0.25 holds out of the voice loop.
4. **Choose automatically.** Use hosted Live when there's enough credit and the gateway is healthy, otherwise use local, and let the user override it in settings.

For read-aloud narration, I wouldn't assume it yet. A correction first: there's no Kokoro in the code. In-browser speech is Supertonic only (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`); OpenAI and Fish voices go through providers.

**Where LFM3 audio should win:** Supertonic only turns text into speech. A local Live mode built on it would chain three separate models: speech-to-text, a text model, then Supertonic. You'd wait for each step in turn, and it can't handle being interrupted. LFM3 audio is one model that listens and speaks, so it can respond while you're still talking and handle interruptions. For Live it's a different kind of thing, not a small upgrade.

**Where Supertonic still holds up:**
- **Size:** Supertonic is about 260 MB (the files listed in `browser-inference.ts`) and already runs in the browser with WebGPU, falling back to WASM. LFM3 audio is about 2.2B parameters, roughly 1.5 GB or more even compressed, and I found no browser runtime for it yet.
- **Narration:** reading a chapter aloud doesn't need conversation, just good, consistent voices. Supertonic's fixed voice embeddings are made for exactly that. I haven't seen anything on LFM3's voice quality, its voice choices, or how it holds up over long passages.

**My suggestion:**

## Why voice fails

The Not Organic gateway's OpenAI key for Live voice is dead, so voice can't start for any account, not just yours. "Disconnected before final usage arrived" is a misleading catch-all the browser shows whenever the socket closes without a proper end-of-session message (`src/utils/live-voice.ts:554`).

**What happens on each attempt:**
1. Twyne's checks all pass. The Railway logs at 08:18 UTC today show `/v1/wallet` 200, `/v1/realtime/consent` 200 and the token exchange 200, so your credit, consent and sign-in are fine.
2. The gateway accepts the Live connection and then tries to open its own connection to OpenAI with `OPENAI_LIVE_API_KEY`.
3. OpenAI rejects that key with **401 `invalid_api_key`**. I confirmed this by testing the gateway's key directly against `wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions`.
4. The gateway's relay (`apps/gateway/src/bun-realtime.ts`) closes the connection without sending an error message, and it logs nothing. Twyne's relay just passes the close through, so the browser lands in its generic "closed early" message.

Both of your attempts at 08:18 closed within half a second. There hasn't been a successful Live session in the last 7 days.

**You weren't charged.** OpenAI never accepted the connection, so the gateway took the "never started" path (`live_not_started`) and released the $0.50 hold.

I think this works, but as a fallback path. It shouldn't replace Live. Here's what I found.

**Where Twyne already is.** Most of the plumbing exists:
- **Desktop app:** it already runs a local model server, `desktop/litert-server.ts`.
- **Local text models:** `evals/run-local-model.ts` already tests LFM2.5-2.6B as the local engine, served through llama.cpp's `llama-server --jinja`.
- **Voice parts:** speech output already runs in the browser (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`). The Live voice desk is separate from the provider: the tools, edit proposals and apply/discard steps live in `live-voice-contract` and `live-voice-workspace`. A local voice model could reuse all of that.

**What I could confirm about LFM3** (the release is a day old, so coverage is thin):
- **Sizes and cost:** the audio model and Omni are about 2B parameters. The hosted API charges $2 per million audio-input tokens and $10 per million audio-output tokens. Liquid says the first response token can arrive about 50ms after speech ends, but that's their best case.
- **Running it locally:** llama.cpp can run the text side, and speech-to-text is still a pending pull request there. Full two-way voice chat currently needs Liquid's Python runtime. I found nothing on running it in the browser (WebGPU/ONNX), and only one third-party blog mentions full-duplex at all.
- **Vision:** you're right that Twyne doesn't need it. Omni would mean downloading vision weights for nothing, so the audio-only model is the better pick.
- **The decision model:** I couldn't confirm "D1" from the sources I found. Can you send me a link?

**How I'd build it:**
1. **Desktop first.** Run LFM3 audio as a local server next to `litert-server` and point the Live relay at it with the same event shape. Live voice would then work offline and cost nothing on desktop.
2. **Web next.** The web version can't run the Python runtime, so voice there has to stay hosted until a WebGPU/ONNX build ships. One caveat on the out-of-credits fallback: it only works if the user has a local runtime (desktop, or a local server they set up).
3. **Use the decision model in place of Jev.** It would run the local `judgement` and `interpret` steps. That takes Jev's 503s and the per-action $0.25 holds out of the voice loop.
4. **Choose automatically.** Use hosted Live when there's enough credit and the gateway is healthy, otherwise use local, and let the user override it in settings.

For live conversation, yes, very likely. For read-aloud narration, I wouldn't assume it yet. A correction first: there's no Kokoro in the code. In-browser speech is Supertonic only (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`); OpenAI and Fish voices go through providers.

**Where LFM3 audio should win:** Supertonic only turns text into speech. A local Live mode built on it would chain three separate models: speech-to-text, a text model, then Supertonic. You'd wait for each step in turn, and it can't handle being interrupted. LFM3 audio is one model that listens and speaks, so it can respond while you're still talking and handle interruptions. For Live it's a different kind of thing, not a small upgrade.

**Where Supertonic still holds up:**
- **Size:** Supertonic is about 260 MB (the files listed in `browser-inference.ts`) and already runs in the browser with WebGPU, falling back to WASM. LFM3 audio is about 2.2B parameters, roughly 1.5 GB or more even compressed, and I found no browser runtime for it yet.
- **Narration:** reading a chapter aloud doesn't need conversation, just good, consistent voices. Supertonic's fixed voice embeddings are made for exactly that. I haven't seen anything on LFM3's voice quality, its voice choices, or how it holds up over long passages.

**My suggestion:**
- Use LFM3 audio for local Live: desktop first, and as the fallback when credits run out.
- Keep Supertonic for in-browser narration until a side-by-side test says otherwise. I can add that test to the LFM3 eval: the same passages through both, judged on clarity, pacing and voice consistency.

If LFM3 wins clearly and someone ships a browser build, replacing Supertonic becomes a simple swap.

agent 2026-10-28T08:28:29.633Z I think this works, but as a fallback path. It shouldn't replace Live. Here's what I found.

**Where Twyne already is.** Most of the plumbing exists:
- **Desktop app:** it already runs a local model server, `desktop/litert-server.ts`.
- **Local text models:** `evals/run-local-model.ts` already tests LFM2.5-2.6B as the local engine, served through llama.cpp's `llama-server --jinja`.
- **Voice parts:** speech output already runs in the browser (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`). The Live voice desk is separate from the provider: the tools, edit proposals and apply/discard steps live in `live-voice-contract` and `live-voice-workspace`. A local voice model could reuse all of that.

**What I could confirm about LFM3** (the release is a day old, so coverage is thin):
- **Sizes and cost:** the audio model and Omni are about 2B parameters. The hosted API charges $2 per million audio-input tokens and $10 per million audio-output tokens. Liquid says the first response token can arrive about 50ms after speech ends, but that's their best case.
- **Running it locally:** llama.cpp can run the text side, and speech-to-text is still a pending pull request there. Full two-way voice chat currently needs Liquid's Python runtime. I found nothing on running it in the browser (WebGPU/ONNX), and only one third-party blog mentions full-duplex at all.
- **Vision:** you're right that Twyne doesn't need it. Omni would mean downloading vision weights for nothing, so the audio-only model is the better pick.
- **The decision model:** I couldn't confirm "D1" from the sources I found. Can you send me a link?

**How I'd build it:**
1. **Desktop first.** Run LFM3 audio as a local server next to `litert-server` and point the Live relay at it with the same event shape. Live voice would then work offline and cost nothing on desktop.
2. **Web next.** The web version can't run the Python runtime, so voice there has to stay hosted until a WebGPU/ONNX build ships. One caveat on the out-of-credits fallback: it only works if the user has a local runtime (desktop, or a local server they set up).
3. **Use the decision model in place of Jev.** It would run the local `judgement` and `interpret` steps. That takes Jev's 503s and the per-action $0.25 holds out of the voice loop.
4. **Choose automatically.** Use hosted Live when there's enough credit and the gateway is healthy, otherwise use local, and let the user override it in settings.

Before building, I'd test it the way `run-local-model.ts` tests LFM2.
--
agent 2026-10-28T08:28:45.801Z For live conversation, yes, very likely. For read-aloud narration, I wouldn't assume it yet. A correction first: there's no Kokoro in the code. In-browser speech is Supertonic only (`src/utils/supertonic-tts.ts`); OpenAI and Fish voices go through providers.

**Where LFM3 audio should win:** Supertonic only turns text into speech. A local Live mode built on it would chain three separate models: speech-to-text, a text model, then Supertonic. You'd wait for each step in turn, and it can't handle being interrupted. LFM3 audio is one model that listens and speaks, so it can respond while you're still talking and handle interruptions. For Live it's a different kind of thing, not a small upgrade.

**Where Supertonic still holds up:**
- **Size:** Supertonic is about 260 MB (the files listed in `browser-inference.ts`) and already runs in the browser with WebGPU, falling back to WASM. LFM3 audio is about 2.2B parameters, roughly 1.5 GB or more even compressed, and I found no browser runtime for it yet.
- **Narration:** reading a chapter aloud doesn't need conversation, just good, consistent voices. Supertonic's fixed voice embeddings are made for exactly that. I haven't seen anything on LFM3's voice quality, its voice choices, or how it holds up over long passages.

**My suggestion:**
- Use LFM3 audio for local Live: desktop first, and as the fallback when credits run out.
- Keep Supertonic for in-browser narration until a side-by-side test says otherwise. I can add that test to the LFM3 eval: the same passages through both, judged on clarity, pacing and voice consistency.

If LFM3 wins clearly and someone ships a browser build, replacing Supertonic becomes a simple swap.
--

<sub>2026-10-20</sub>

- Let the editors read on their own: a draft they have not seen is read once it
  reaches 500 words, then again after 200 new or rewritten words and a pause.

  background, keeping their notes beside later quick grades.

content.text:
I've pushed v0.26.0 to main, and Railway is building it for production now. I'll confirm once that deploy finishes.

**What went out:**
- **Persona note card:** the compact two-box design with icon controls and compact warnings.
- **Faces on note anchors:** each anchor shows the persona's face, or your profile photo, in their colour. This came from the other thread, which couldn't take screenshots. When I checked it here, the face showed up as a tiny squeezed strip instead of a face. The editor's image styling was causing that, so I fixed it.
- **Your dropdown bug:** the "canonical uses left alone" disclosure in the Organization & Flow lens no longer closes when you hover its passages. I added a test that hovers the rows, and the 10 living desk tests pass, run twice.
